question: In late 2011, a genre cinema website run by a single blogger—who had amassed hundreds of reviews spanning horror, exploitation, and martial arts from around the world—published an introductory piece about a long-running Japanese film series. That series, centered on a blind swordsman from the Edo period, consisted of over two dozen films produced across more than a decade, with a standalone sequel appearing after a lengthy hiatus. Unlike its Hong Kong counterparts, the series avoided spectacular arterial sprays, favoring a more restrained samurai aesthetic. The character was immortalized by an actor whose heartfelt performance resonated deeply with common people and the oppressed, earning immense popularity over several decades. The same studio that launched this blind-swordsman franchise also gave birth to another beloved series featuring a giant turtle creature that first appeared in the mid-1960s. During its postwar golden age, the studio had produced internationally groundbreaking films: one that won the top prize at a major European festival, and another that became the first color film from Japan to win major awards in both the United States and Europe. The studio itself had been founded in the early 1940s, amid the Second World War, through a government-mandated merger, with a novelist as its initial president; later, a seasoned film executive guided it through its most productive decades. After declaring bankruptcy in the early 1970s, the studio was briefly resurrected by a publishing house established in the mid-1950s that would later own a renowned animation studio, but it was ultimately sold and folded into the film division of a major publisher that had originated in the 1970s and absorbed another historic studio at the dawn of the 21st century. What was the name of this studio?

question: Back in the late 19th century, a legal scholar founded a quarterly journal that would become one of the oldest in the English-speaking world, held an Oxford professorship for twenty years, and wrote a pioneering treatise on contract law comparing Roman, American, and continental principles. That volume, containing several hundred pages, was eventually digitized by an organization founded in the mid-1990s by a technologist who had previously worked on early search technologies at a supercomputer company, co-founded an information system acquired by an ISP, and co-founded a web navigation company whose toolbar was bought by Amazon. The digitization of this particular volume required over 200 minutes of OCR processing. Around the early 2010s, the digitizing organization outsourced a significant part of its scanning work to Datum Data Co., while it operates more than thirty scanning centers across five countries. What is the exact title of this legal case collection?

The scrolls, numbering about 1,800 and primarily philosophical texts in Greek, are kept at an institution that also preserves approximately 1,800 papyrus papers and drawings from Herculaneum, housed in the eastern wing of a Baroque and Neo-Classical palace built in 1600 as a residence for Spanish viceroys. That same institution safeguards a collection of over 300 classical sculptures—including a 3-meter-tall Roman marble Hercules from the second largest ancient Roman public baths, all copies of Greek originals—and the autograph corpus of Giacomo Leopardi. Because the scrolls are too fragile to unroll, researchers rely on digital X-ray techniques. A researcher who won a prize for detecting ink traces in these scrolls using AI laid the groundwork, and later a university student from Nebraska applied machine learning to identify a Greek word meaning "purple" within an unopened scroll. This breakthrough earned the student a monetary award from a 2023 competition that offers a $700,000 grand prize for deciphering passages from scrolls carbonized by a volcanic eruption. What was the exact dollar amount of that award?

A collections specialist at this museum who works with this historical currency collection authored a blog post in late 2020. This post examines how emergency currency issued by European municipalities during the post-WWI economic crisis—often featuring elaborate artistic designs—served as cultural artifacts, and specifically analyzes how such currency from various regional communities incorporated guardian creatures and legendary figures as messages of comfort or behavioral warnings during uncertainty, while also exploring how communities used these everyday objects featuring supernatural beings to maintain cultural continuity during national economic instability. What is the title of this blog post?

question: In a paper published in the mid‑20th century in a monthly journal that has been owned by the American Astronomical Society since 1941, an astronomer described a celestial object with a perfect halo of about 17 arc seconds in radius. The observatory also employed over 140 women computers who studied those plates, and now maintains a digital platform linking the plates to their notebooks, as well as a project transcribing those notebooks with help from a crowdsourcing platform launched in 2013 that has engaged tens of thousands of volunteers, and a global citizen science platform used for its “Star Notes” initiative that completed its first phase in mid‑2022. The collection also features contemporary art, including a large‑scale lenticular photography installation in the Boston subway by an associate professor at a women’s college, honoring a pioneering female astronomer. The volume eventually came into the possession of an American businessman and diplomat, a Harvard alumnus, who donated it to his alma mater’s prestigious rare-book library, where it remained for nearly a century. In the early 2020s, a French publisher specializing in annotated re-editions of forgotten works brought out a new edition. A few years before that, however, the library had published a blog post announcing that scientific analysis had definitively identified the binding material. That analysis employed a protein-identification technique developed in the early-to-mid 1990s, with key contributions from a researcher at a pioneering California biotechnology company that created protein-based therapeutics. The technique’s workflow uses instruments like MALDI-TOF mass spectrometers and relies on a search engine called Aldente, accessible via the ExPASy proteomics server, where users specify parameters such as enzyme cleavage sites and taxonomic scope. The blog post itself, later condemned by the library for its flippant and sensational tone, triggered global headlines before being taken down; the institution subsequently voiced regret and revised its policies roughly a decade afterward. What was the full, exact title of that controversial blog post?

The journal's founding editor-in-chief was a Dutch botanist born in the mid-1970s, educated at Utrecht University, who earned his PhD in Finland and specializes in plant classification. This entomologist, who earned degrees from a northernmost UC campus and a Southern California public university founded in 1949, with research on a hemipteran insect's temperature-dependent aggregating behavior, also taught at a Los Angeles County community college established in the late 1960s and helped create insect fairs at a major natural history museum (founded 1913, with 35 million specimens) that attracted over 100,000 visitors. He pioneered a 'Bug Art' technique, using live insects to transfer paint onto canvas, which went viral through a defunct Turner Broadcasting digital platform with over 15 million views and was the subject of a documentary. He recreated Vincent van Gogh's 'Starry Night' as a piece titled 'Starry Night Saturday', exhibited at a New Mexican gallery founded in 2018 between Albuquerque and Santa Fe, and included in a 2017 art book of insect-inspired works by 39 contemporary artists. His television appearances included NBC's long-running late-night talk show (1962–1992), another late-1980s late-night program, and an Emmy-nominated 1992 episode about arachnophobia. He was featured in The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, the same major Western newspaper, and a children's science magazine from Cricket Media. He served as a consultant for a California vector control agency formed in 1952 and on the board of a monarch butterfly program. His bug art was also documented in a short documentary and a 2017 miniature book by Karen Klein, part of a 30-volume insect dreams collection. The article also described how his pet tarantula helped thousands of schoolchildren overcome their fear of insects, and it included his criticism of a nearly 700,000-acre national forest near Los Angeles, established in 1892, for lacking formal plans to preserve indigenous insects.

question: What is the title of the investigative journalism article that was published around the early 1970s in a prominent American news magazine founded in 1923, which originally came out weekly but later switched to a biweekly schedule? This article uncovered how an American novelist born in 1930 fabricated an autobiography of a reclusive billionaire industrialist. The industrialist had inherited a major oil drilling company in the early 1920s and built a vast business empire across aviation, film, and real estate. He founded an aerospace and defense contractor in the early 1930s and set multiple aviation records, including circling the globe in under four days. He also designed an aircraft that, equipped with a powerful radial engine from the world's second largest commercial aircraft engine maker, broke the world landplane speed record in the mid-1930s—officially observed by a trailblazing female aviator who later vanished over the Pacific—and later achieved a transcontinental speed record that was eventually surpassed by a Hollywood stunt pilot who perished in a movie-set crash. This aircraft was later donated to the Smithsonian Institution. The industrialist, who suffered from obsessive-compulsive disorder, became increasingly reclusive and bought properties in a famous Nevada gambling hub. He had a brief marriage to a Houston socialite in the mid-1920s. The fake autobiography was created by plagiarizing the manuscript of a West Coast investigative reporter who had previously written magazine articles about the billionaire and had served as ghostwriter for the memoir of the billionaire's longtime chief of staff—a financial adviser who managed the empire for over three decades. The plagiarized manuscript traveled through a Hollywood film producer and a New York literary agent before landing at a major New York publishing house established in 1924, one of the "Big Five" English-language publishers. The article also detailed the legal confession of the novelist after the hoax was detected by comparing the two manuscripts side by side. What is the name of this article?

question: Back in 2013, a musician embarked on a decade-long quest to reconstruct three microtonal instruments first devised by a maverick American composer in the mid-20th century. This journey, documented in a detailed Fretboard Journal blog post, involved releasing an album of original compositions on a replica of the composer's modified 1920s parlor guitar, which featured high stainless-steel frets. Collaborating across continents, the project culminated in a new replica instrument, structurally modified by an Australian luthier with over twenty years of experience, working in a regional city, and financially supported by an experimental music ensemble. Unlike the original, this replica was built on a large-bodied Japanese acoustic guitar from the late 1970s to improve bass response. That Japanese guitar, a clone of a classic American dreadnought model, has a market history of several hundred transactions with average sale prices in the low hundreds. It can be heard on a 2024 album of experimental microtonal music, where it is fitted with an award-winning bridge plate pickup and uses coated strings. The string coating technology traces back to a mid-1990s innovation program at a company founded in 1958 that revolutionized waterproof breathable fabrics; the coating was developed by a researcher who used accelerometers to ensure acoustic transparency, and it incorporates a special plating to extend the life of unwound steel strings. Over the years, this replica guitar was upgraded multiple times, gaining additional frets to expand its musical range. What is the title of the blog post that recounts this entire endeavor?
